rv.q: Exquisite moments like that, hilarious and scalding, bear the hallmark not only of Harrison but also of David Cromer, who directed “The Antiquities” with Caitlin Sullivan.
When Harrison zooms all the way into the specifics of a scene, especially in those vignettes with Cheung's mother and Spahn's coder, his work sings most cleanly, where naturalism melds with sly wit.
It all makes for a potent and uncomfortably convincing vision of where we are headed.
Questions of love and freedom, ethics and goals, history and foresight, and sisterhood and marriage are thoughtfully explored with great humor, and through a fantastic cast.
The Antiquities is a striking accomplishment as a piece of intricate, thought-provoking playwriting; it’s given a gorgeous, intelligent production here.
The Antiquities gets credit for conceptual creativity and topicality. Even though it doesn't break new ground when it comes to the power and perils of technology, it grips with a quiet urgency.
“The Antiquities,” which imagines a future in which human beings are no longer welcome by the creatures they created, started to outwear its own.
Although The Antiquities is a very dark ride, it is a very timely cautionary tale as Artificial Intelligence increasingly invades our human world.
The material, however, is too skeletal to allow for more than superficial characterizations that do little more than give outline impressions of the people they’re playing.
The show is absolutely fascinating with more data points than I can analyze.
Some exhibits are more compelling than others.
My biggest reservation about The Antiquities is how the tidy, schematic nature of its construction sometimes undercuts its power, and even works against its overarching pro-humanity message.
Jordan Harrison focuses on humanity's role...intensely clever and prescient warning shot.

cn.t: Harrison's intelligent, timely exploration of AI and humanity's relationship with technology impresses with its ambition and ideas, though critics find the episodic structure more essay-like than dramatically compelling.

vr.q: It’s one of those pieces that I'm glad I saw, but I only need to experience once.
